title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Utterances 226-243 (sarcophagus chamber, west gable)
source: Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, sarcophagus chamber, west gable (photograph: L. F. Husson for A. Piankoff 1968, via Pyramid Texts Online) + TLA transliteration (ed. D. Topmann, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of S. A. B. Mercer (1952, public domain in the US)
description: The Pyramid Texts on the west gable of the sarcophagus chamber in the pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BCE), utterance by utterance, with the TLA transliteration and Mercer's English.
introduction:
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest large body of Egyptian religious writing: spells, called utterances, for the resurrection of the dead king, his protection, his meals and his ascent to the sky, cut in vertical columns of hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial apartments of late Old Kingdom pyramids. The pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, the last king of the 5th Dynasty (about 2375-2345 BCE), is the first to carry them. Its sarcophagus chamber, the passage to the antechamber, the antechamber and the corridor hold 649 numbered columns of text; this library gives every column, wall by wall, in seventeen entries (227 different utterances, some of them inscribed more than once).

This entry is the west gable of the sarcophagus chamber: 40 columns of hieroglyphs, Sethe's W 300-340, which follow each other from the right-hand (north) edge of the photograph. It holds the utterances 226, 227, 228, 229, 230, 231, 232, 233, 234, 235, 236, 238, 237, 239, 240, 241, 242, 243. Sethe's numbering skips W 318; the gable has 40 columns.

Each section is one utterance. The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Doris Topmann), with Sethe's Unas column number (W) before each column; a number ending in 'a' marks the offering label at the foot of a column. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, damaged signs in half brackets. The English is Samuel A. B. Mercer's translation of 1952. Mercer translates Sethe's composite text made from all the pyramids that have an utterance, so his wording can include clauses that are not in the Unas copy, and his section numbers (134a, 134b ...) are Sethe's paragraph numbers, not column numbers; he writes 'N.' where the wall has the king's name. The photograph shows the whole wall; each section's note gives its columns counted from the edge where the text on that wall begins.
translator_notes: Mercer's separate headings, postscripts and variants taken from other pyramids are left out.
Letters follow the sacred-texts transcription of Mercer: ȝ stands for aleph and ‘ for ayin; letters underlined in the printed book are given as ḏ, ṯ, ẖ.
Sethe's section numbers are kept as printed in that transcription, including a few misprints (for example '146.' for 141b in Utterance 215).
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

225bwhen a toothless (?) calf born on pasture-land is encircled.
225cEarth, devour that which has come forth from thee. Monster (beast), lie down, glide away.
226aA servant (holy person) who belongs to the Ennead (pelican) is fallen in water.
226bSerpent, turn over that Rē‘ may see thee.

translation.text:
230aTo say: Be thy two poison-glands in the ground; be thy two rows of ribs in the hole.
230bPour out the liquid. The two kites stand there.
230cThy mouth is closed by the hangman's tool; the mouth of the hangman's tool is closed by the mȝfd.t (lynx).
230dThe one made tired is bitten by a serpent.
231aO Rē‘, N. has bitten the earth; N. has bitten Geb.
231bN. has bitten the father of him who bit him.
231cThis is the being who has bitten N., (though) N. did not bite him.
232aIt is he who is come against N., (though) N. does not go against him;
232bthe second moment after he saw N., the second moment after he perceived N.
232cIf thou bitest N., he will make one (piece) of thee; if thou regardest N., he will make two of thee.
233aThe n‘w-serpent (male) is bitten by the n‘.t-serpent (female); the n‘.t-serpent is bitten by the n‘w-serpent.
233bHeaven is protected magically; earth is protected magically; the "manly" who is behind mankind is protected magically.
234aThe god whose head is blind is protected magically; thou thyself, scorpion, art protected magically.
234bThese are the two knots (charm) of Elephantiné which are in the mouth of Osiris,
234cwhich Horus knotted concerning the backbone.
